    Benchmarking gt_clumppling() against the python clumppling

    clumppling_benchmark.Rmd

    gt_clumppling() aligns the clusters of replicate runs of ADMIXTURE-like analyses, and groups the runs into modes, with the method of clumppling (Liu, Kopelman & Rosenberg 2024). Its R and C++ code is ported, with modifications, from the python package clumppling (version 2.0.10, by Xiran Liu), which previous versions of tidygenclust ran through reticulate. This article compares the two implementations: do they give the same results, and how long do they take?

    The comparison uses the two example datasets of the python clumppling, which are also analysed in the paper that describes it (Liu, Kopelman & Rosenberg 2024), and which tidygenclust includes as gt_admix objects (in inst/extdata):

    • capeverde: 200 runs of ADMIXTURE (50 for each K from 2 to 5) on the Cape Verde data of Verdu et al. (2017), with 399 individuals (44 Cape Verdeans, and 355 individuals from British, French, Iberian, Gambian and Mandenka populations);
    • chicken: 60 runs of STRUCTURE (20 for each of K = 17, 19 and 21) on the chicken data of Rosenberg et al. (2001), with 600 chickens from 20 breeds.

    Results

    Summary

    • With the Q matrices already in memory, on the 200 runs of the capeverde data (399 individuals, K = 2 to 5), gt_clumppling() took 0.077 s and the python implementation 17 s, about 215 times longer. On the 60 runs of the chicken data (600 individuals, K = 17, 19 and 21), they took 0.23 s and 3.9 s.
    • Starting from Q files adds the time taken to read them: on the 200 capeverde runs, 0.26 s and 17 s. In R, reading the files takes longer than gt_clumppling() itself.
    • From the command line, each implementation also has to start, and load its packages: about 0.99 s for R and 2.1 s for python. With few runs, this is most of the time, and the difference shrinks: with 5 runs for each K, 1.1 s and 2.8 s. With 200 runs, it is still 1.3 s against 18 s.
    • The two implementations found the same modes in 4 of the 5 datasets. Where the modes were the same, their aligned ancestry proportions differed by at most 2.2e-16. On the chicken data, the modes were the same for K = 21 only, as expected (see below).

    Do they give the same results?

    Both implementations were run with the default options (use_rep = TRUE, merge = TRUE, cd_method = "louvain", use_best_pair = TRUE) and the same seed. Each implementation runs the same code whether the Q matrices are in memory, read from Q files or the analysis is run from the command line (see below), so the results were compared once, with the Q matrices in memory:

    Number of modes found by each implementation, the values of K for which the modes (the runs in each mode) are the same, whether the representative runs of the modes are the same, and, where all the modes are the same, the largest absolute differences between the aligned ancestry proportions of the modes, and between the costs of the alignments across K.
    Dataset Runs Individuals K Modes (R) Modes (python) K with the same modes Same representatives Largest difference (modes) Largest difference (costs)
    capeverde_5 20 399 2, 3, 4, 5 9 9 2, 3, 4, 5 yes 2.2e-16 4.2e-17
    capeverde_10 40 399 2, 3, 4, 5 6 6 2, 3, 4, 5 yes 2.2e-16 2.8e-17
    capeverde_20 80 399 2, 3, 4, 5 6 6 2, 3, 4, 5 yes 2.2e-16 3.5e-18
    capeverde_50 200 399 2, 3, 4, 5 7 7 2, 3, 4, 5 yes 2.2e-16 4.2e-17
    chicken_20 60 600 17, 19, 21 8 7 21 no - -

    Where the modes are the same, the remaining differences are rounding errors. Grouping runs into modes uses community detection (the Louvain method, by default), which draws random numbers. gt_clumppling() draws them from R’s generator, so the same seed does not give the same random choices as in python. This does not change the modes when the community structure of the runs is clear, as in the capeverde data. It can when the structure is ambiguous, as for K = 17 and 19 in the chicken data, where the modes found by python itself change with the seed. The test suite of tidygenclust checks that, given the same modes, the two implementations give the same results on these data.

    How long do they take?

    The two implementations are typically used in different ways. In R, the Q matrices are usually already in memory, in a gt_admix object returned by gt_admixture() or by tidypopgen::read_q_files(), and gt_clumppling() returns its results as an R object. The python clumppling is usually run as a command-line tool, which starts python, loads its packages, reads the Q files, and writes its results to files. Timing gt_clumppling() on a gt_admix object against the command-line tool would flatter gt_clumppling(). So we timed each implementation in three settings:

    • In memory: the Q matrices are already in memory, and R or python is already running, with the packages loaded. This times the method alone. In python, the Q matrices are converted to numpy arrays before the timing starts, and the results are left as python objects, so the time taken to pass data between R and python (with reticulate) is not included.
    • From Q files: as above, but starting from a directory of Q files, one for each run. In R, they are read with tidypopgen::read_q_files(). In python, they are read by clumppling’s own parser, which writes the processed matrices to a directory and reads them back, as the command-line tool does.
    • From the command line: each run is a new process, which starts R or python, loads the packages, reads the Q files, and saves the results. In R, this is a script run with Rscript, which loads tidygenclust and saves the results with saveRDS(). In python, it is the command-line tool of clumppling, without figures (-v False).

    The last setting is the closest to the time a user waits, but the two implementations still do slightly different things: the command-line tool of clumppling writes more output than saveRDS() (the processed Q files, the alignment of every pair of runs, the modes and their statistics, and a log).

    Median time (s) of 5 runs of each implementation, in each setting, and ratio of the times of python and gt_clumppling().
    Setting Dataset Runs K gt_clumppling() (s) python (s) Speed-up
    In memory capeverde_5 20 2, 3, 4, 5 0.02 0.54 27
    capeverde_10 40 2, 3, 4, 5 0.02 0.81 41
    capeverde_20 80 2, 3, 4, 5 0.029 2.8 97
    capeverde_50 200 2, 3, 4, 5 0.077 17 215
    chicken_20 60 17, 19, 21 0.23 3.9 17
    From Q files capeverde_5 20 2, 3, 4, 5 0.037 0.57 15
    capeverde_10 40 2, 3, 4, 5 0.056 0.89 16
    capeverde_20 80 2, 3, 4, 5 0.098 3.2 32
    capeverde_50 200 2, 3, 4, 5 0.26 17 65
    chicken_20 60 17, 19, 21 0.51 4.6 9
    From the command line capeverde_5 20 2, 3, 4, 5 1.1 2.8 3
    capeverde_10 40 2, 3, 4, 5 1.1 3.1 3
    capeverde_20 80 2, 3, 4, 5 1.2 5.6 5
    capeverde_50 200 2, 3, 4, 5 1.3 18 14
    chicken_20 60 17, 19, 21 1.5 7.7 5

    With many runs, most of the time goes into aligning every pair of runs with the same K, so the time grows roughly with the square of the number of runs for each K. For each pair, clumppling solves an integer linear program with GLPK (through cvxpy), whereas gt_clumppling() solves the same problem exactly as a linear assignment problem, with the Hungarian algorithm in C++.

    Reading the 200 capeverde Q files took about 0.18 s in R (tidypopgen::read_q_files() reads each file with read.table()), more than gt_clumppling() itself, but little compared with the time of the python implementation, whose own parser took about 0.29 s.

    From the command line, starting R and loading tidygenclust took about 0.99 s, and starting python and loading clumppling (with numpy, cvxpy, cdlib and matplotlib) about 2.1 s (medians of 5 runs, without doing anything else). This sets a floor to the times of both implementations, which dominates with few runs. The rest of the time from the command line is within about a second of the time from Q files, so writing the results takes little time, although clumppling writes more of them.

    How the benchmark was run

    The benchmark is run with the script vignettes/articles/code/clumppling_benchmark.R (in the source code of the package), which saves its results in vignettes/articles/data/clumppling_benchmark; this article reads them from there. The code below is taken from that script.

    The python implementation is run with the wrapper that previous versions of tidygenclust used, which is now used to create the reference results of the tests (data-raw/clumppling/py_clumppling.R). It runs in the conda environment created by data-raw/clumppling/setup_clumppling_env.sh, with clumppling 2.0.10 and pinned versions of its dependencies:

    library(tidygenclust)
start_time <- Sys.time()
out_dir <- "data/clumppling_benchmark"
dir.create(out_dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
# each implementation is timed n_repeats times on each dataset and in each
# setting, after a first run (not timed) that loads its code and gives the
# results compared
n_repeats <- 5
seed <- 1L
    # py_clumppling() runs the python implementation on a gt_admix object, with
# the same arguments as gt_clumppling(); the wrapper is sourced from the
# root of the package, where it finds its python module
withr::with_dir(
  "../..",
  source("data-raw/clumppling/py_clumppling.R")
)
# the same python module, returning python objects instead of converting
# them to R objects, to time the python code alone
py_module <- reticulate::import_from_path(
  "py_rclumppling",
  path = "../../data-raw/clumppling",
  convert = FALSE
)
# the executables of python (in the conda environment) and R, for the runs
# from the command line
python <- reticulate::py_exe()
rscript <- file.path(R.home("bin"), "Rscript")

    The datasets are the example datasets of clumppling (see the introduction), and subsets of the capeverde data with fewer runs for each K. Each is also written as a directory of Q files, and converted to numpy arrays:

    # the example datasets of clumppling, included in tidygenclust: 200 runs of
# ADMIXTURE (50 for each K from 2 to 5) on the Cape Verde data of Verdu et
# al. (2017), with 399 individuals (capeverde), and 60 runs of STRUCTURE (20
# for each of K = 17, 19 and 21) on the chicken data of Rosenberg et al.
# (2001), with 600 chickens
capeverde <- readRDS(
  system.file("extdata", "capeverde_admix.rds", package = "tidygenclust")
)
chicken <- readRDS(
  system.file("extdata", "chicken_admix.rds", package = "tidygenclust")
)
# the first n runs of each K of a gt_admix object
first_runs <- function(x, n) {
  keep <- sort(unlist(lapply(split(seq_along(x$k), x$k), utils::head, n)))
  x$k <- x$k[keep]
  x$Q <- x$Q[keep]
  x
}
# capeverde with 5, 10, 20 and 50 runs for each K, and chicken
datasets <- list(
  capeverde_5 = first_runs(capeverde, 5),
  capeverde_10 = first_runs(capeverde, 10),
  capeverde_20 = first_runs(capeverde, 20),
  capeverde_50 = capeverde,
  chicken_20 = chicken
)
# each dataset as a directory of Q files (one for each run, with one row for
# each individual and one column for each cluster, as written by ADMIXTURE),
# and as a python list of numpy arrays
write_q_files <- function(x, q_dir) {
  dir.create(q_dir)
  for (i in seq_along(x$Q)) {
    utils::write.table(
      as.matrix(x$Q[[i]]),
      file.path(q_dir, sprintf("run%03d.Q", i)),
      row.names = FALSE,
      col.names = FALSE
    )
  }
  q_dir
}
to_numpy <- function(x) {
  reticulate::r_to_py(lapply(x$Q, function(q) {
    reticulate::np_array(
      matrix(as.numeric(q), nrow = nrow(q)),
      dtype = "float64",
      order = "C"
    )
  }))
}
inputs <- lapply(names(datasets), function(name) {
  list(
    admix = datasets[[name]],
    q_dir = write_q_files(datasets[[name]], file.path(tempdir(), name)),
    q_py = to_numpy(datasets[[name]])
  )
})
names(inputs) <- names(datasets)

    The results of the two implementations are compared with:

    # compare the results of the two implementations: their modes (the runs of
# each mode, overall and for each K), their representatives, and, if the
# modes are the same, the largest differences between their aligned modes
# and their costs across K
compare_results <- function(r, py) {
  # the modes (named e.g. K2M1) of the values of K that match the pattern
  modes_of <- function(res, pattern) {
    modes <- res$mode_replicates[grep(pattern, names(res$mode_replicates))]
    lapply(modes, as.integer)
  }
  same_modes <- identical(modes_of(r, ""), modes_of(py, ""))
  same_modes_k <- Filter(function(k) {
    pattern <- paste0("^K", k, "M")
    identical(modes_of(r, pattern), modes_of(py, pattern))
  }, r$K_range)
  # (the elements of both lists are matched by name)
  max_diff <- function(a, b) {
    b <- b[names(a)]
    max(abs(unlist(lapply(a, as.matrix)) - unlist(lapply(b, as.matrix))))
  }
  data.frame(
    n_modes_r = length(r$mode_replicates),
    n_modes_python = length(py$mode_replicates),
    same_modes = same_modes,
    same_modes_k = paste(same_modes_k, collapse = ", "),
    same_representatives = identical(
      r$mode_stats$Representative,
      py$mode_stats$Representative
    ),
    max_diff_aligned = if (same_modes) {
      max_diff(r$aligned_modes, py$aligned_modes)
    } else {
      NA
    },
    max_diff_cost = if (same_modes) {
      max_diff(r$cost_acrossK, py$cost_acrossK)
    } else {
      NA
    }
  )
}

    The runs that are timed, in each setting, are:

    # run a command, stopping if it fails
run_command <- function(command, args) {
  status <- system2(command, args, stdout = FALSE, stderr = FALSE)
  if (status != 0) {
    stop("Failed: ", command, " ", paste(args, collapse = " "))
  }
}
# the timed runs of each implementation, in each setting, on an input (a
# dataset as a gt_admix object, a directory of Q files and numpy arrays)
run_r <- list(
  # the Q matrices are in a gt_admix object
  memory = function(input) {
    gt_clumppling(input$admix, seed = seed)
  },
  # the Q files are read with tidypopgen::read_q_files()
  files = function(input) {
    gt_clumppling(tidypopgen::read_q_files(input$q_dir), seed = seed)
  },
  # a new R process loads tidygenclust, reads the Q files, and saves the
  # results in an rds file
  command_line = function(input) {
    out <- tempfile(fileext = ".rds")
    on.exit(unlink(out))
    run_command(rscript, c("-e", shQuote(sprintf(
      paste(
        "library(tidygenclust);",
        "res <- gt_clumppling(tidypopgen::read_q_files('%s'), seed = %d);",
        "saveRDS(res, '%s')"
      ),
      input$q_dir, seed, out
    ))))
  }
)
run_python <- list(
  # the Q matrices are numpy arrays (converted from R before the timing),
  # and the results are python objects (not converted to R)
  memory = function(input) {
    py_module$clumppling_run(Q_list = input$q_py, random_seed = seed)
  },
  # the Q files are read by clumppling's own parser, which writes the
  # processed matrices to a directory and reads them back
  files = function(input) {
    processed_dir <- tempfile()
    on.exit(unlink(processed_dir, recursive = TRUE))
    py_module$clumppling_run(
      input_dir = input$q_dir,
      processed_dir = processed_dir,
      random_seed = seed
    )
  },
  # the command-line tool of clumppling, without figures, which reads the Q
  # files and writes its results to a directory
  command_line = function(input) {
    out <- tempfile()
    on.exit(unlink(out, recursive = TRUE))
    run_command(python, c(
      "-m", "clumppling", "-i", shQuote(input$q_dir), "-o", shQuote(out),
      "-f", "admixture", "-v", "False", "--random_seed", seed
    ))
  }
)

    Each implementation is run on each dataset once in memory, to compare the results, and once from the Q files, and then timed 5 times in each setting:

    timings <- list()
agreement <- list()
for (name in names(inputs)) {
  input <- inputs[[name]]
  x <- input$admix
  message("Running ", name)
  # a first run of each implementation in memory, compared, and a first run
  # from the Q files, neither timed
  res_r <- suppressMessages(gt_clumppling(x, seed = seed))
  res_py <- py_clumppling(x, seed = seed)
  agreement[[name]] <- data.frame(
    dataset = name,
    n_runs = length(x$Q),
    n_individuals = nrow(x$Q[[1]]),
    k_values = paste(sort(unique(x$k)), collapse = ", "),
    compare_results(res_r, res_py)
  )
  invisible(suppressMessages(run_r$files(input)))
  invisible(run_python$files(input))
  # then n_repeats timed runs of each, in each setting
  for (setting in names(run_r)) {
    for (i in seq_len(n_repeats)) {
      seconds_r <- system.time(
        suppressMessages(run_r[[setting]](input))
      )[["elapsed"]]
      seconds_py <- system.time(run_python[[setting]](input))[["elapsed"]]
      timings[[paste(name, setting, i)]] <- data.frame(
        dataset = name,
        setting = setting,
        repeat_run = i,
        implementation = c("r", "python"),
        seconds = c(seconds_r, seconds_py)
      )
    }
  }
}
timings <- do.call(rbind, timings)
agreement <- do.call(rbind, agreement)

    Finally, the time taken to start R or python and load the packages is timed on its own:

    # the time taken to start R and load tidygenclust, and to start python and
# load the code of the command-line tool of clumppling
startup <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(n_repeats), function(i) {
  data.frame(
    repeat_run = i,
    implementation = c("r", "python"),
    seconds = c(
      system.time(
        run_command(rscript, c("-e", shQuote("library(tidygenclust)")))
      )[["elapsed"]],
      system.time(
        run_command(python, c("-c", shQuote("import clumppling.__main__")))
      )[["elapsed"]]
    )
  )
}))

    Running the benchmark again

    Install tidygenclust with R CMD INSTALL, rather than loading it with devtools::load_all(), which compiles its C++ code without optimisation. Create the conda environment with the python implementation (from the root of the package):

    bash data-raw/clumppling/setup_clumppling_env.sh

    or set CLUMPPLING_REFERENCE_ENV to the name of another conda environment with the same versions of the python packages. Then run, from vignettes/articles, on an otherwise idle machine:

    cd vignettes/articles
Rscript code/clumppling_benchmark.R

    This takes a few minutes. Then render this article again.
